column2: The fourth prefatory discussion: on the effect of the air on human character

We have seen that, as a general rule, lightness, flightiness and a great deal of exuberance belong to the character of the black peoples (al-Sūdān), so that you find them passionately fond of dancing to every rhythm and described as foolish in every region. The true reason for this is that it has been established in its proper place in philosophy that the nature of joy and gladness is the spreading of the animal spirit and its diffusion, while the nature of sorrow is the opposite, namely the spirit’s contraction and condensation. It has also been established that heat diffuses the air and the vapor, rarefies it and increases its quantity. For this reason the intoxicated person finds joy and gladness beyond expression. This comes from the innate heat that enters the vapor of the spirit in the heart, which the force of wine rouses in the spirit from its temperament, so that the spirit spreads out and the nature of joy comes about. In the same way we find that those who take their pleasure in the baths, when they breathe the air there and the heat of the air reaches their spirits and warms them, feel joy come over them, and sometimes many of them are moved to burst into song, which arises from gladness.

And since the black peoples live in the hot zone, and heat took hold of their temperaments and of the origin of their generation, their spirits contain heat in proportion to their bodies and their zone. Compared with the spirits of the people of the fourth zone, their spirits are therefore hotter, and so more diffused, and so quicker to joy and gladness and more expansive; and flightiness follows in the wake of these. In the same way the people of the coastal countries also come close to them, though only a little: because the air there is doubled in heat by the lights and rays reflected onto it from the surface of the sea, their share of the consequences of heat, in joy and lightness, is found to be greater than in the lands of the Tells (al-tulūl) and the cold mountains. We also find a little of this among the people of the Jarīd lands of the third zone, because heat is abundant in them and in their air, since they lie deep in the south, far from the farmlands and the Tells. Consider this also in the people of Egypt, which lies at the same latitude as the Jarīd lands or close to it: see how joy, lightness and heedlessness of consequences prevail among them, so that they store up neither the provisions of their year nor those of their month, and most of their food comes from their markets.

And since Fez, among the lands of the Maghrib, is the reverse of it in being deep in the cold Tells, see how its people are downcast, with the bowed look of sorrow, and how they go to excess in considering consequences, so that a man among them will store up two years’ food in grains of wheat and go early to the markets to buy his food for the day, for fear that something might be taken from his store. Follow this through the zones and countries and you will find in character an effect of the qualities of the air; and God is the Creator, the All-Knowing. Al-Masʿūdī took up the inquiry into the reason for the lightness of the black peoples, their flightiness and the abundance of exuberance among them, and tried to explain it, but he offered nothing more than that he reported from Galen and Yaʿqūb ibn Isḥāq al-Kindī that this is due to the weakness of their brains and the weakness of their intellects that arises from it. This is a statement with no substance and no proof in it. “God guides whom He wills to a straight path” (2: 213).
